topic: multi-agent systems; robotic safety; formal verification; agent reliability
status: candidate research opportunity from four cross-year random full-text audits and one peer-reviewed systematic-review abstract; related gap already recognized in prior literature, so not a novelty claim
claim: In this sampled agent_reliability_security slice, safety/reliability claims range from simulation behavior, formal guarantees under a finite model, conceptual proposals, to preliminary optimization architectures. Those are different evidence strengths and cannot be pooled as a common reliability outcome. A focused follow-up is to measure the assurance chain from requirement adequacy through model verification, implementation conformance, fault-injected simulation, and physical/operational transfer, while recording the claim each stage actually supports.
positive_evidence: The 2016 robotic transport paper checks safety/liveness properties in a finite model and maps them to a C# service-based simulation, demonstrating concrete model-level verification rather than only a conceptual architecture.
The 2011 opinion-dynamics paper performs controlled parameter sweeps with ten repeated runs per scenario and exposes nonlinear dependence on tolerance, broadcast reach, and an unreached-agent group.

The 2023 ACM TOSEM systematic review abstract reports a rigorously structured review and explicitly identifies measurement, benchmark, and industrial-applicability evidence gaps in the broader RAS V&V literature.
counterevidence: Formal verification is an established and substantive research line; the 2016 sample paper verifies properties of its stated model, so the opportunity is not to replace or dismiss formal methods.

The 2023 systematic review means broad claims about missing robotics-validation evidence are already recognized and cannot be claimed as novel from this sample; the useful contribution must be a targeted, operationally measurable chain and cross-system test.
The 2011 opinion simulation is a what-if analysis tied to selected assumptions, not causal evidence about real political outcomes; nonlinear results are not general population predictions.

The 2024 FMECA position paper labels its AMAS implementation preliminary and does not provide empirical results, while the 2019 personal-universes paper is conceptual and assumes away value extraction. They should not be used as measured safety outcomes.

sources.title: Testing, Validation, and Verification of Robotic and Autonomous Systems: A Systematic Review
sources.sections: publisher abstract; full article not audited in this follow-up

falsifiable_test: For representative safety-critical agent/robot systems, preregister stakeholder-requirement adequacy review, formal property verification, model-to-code trace/refinement conformance, simulator fault injection, and physical/operational trials. Report property/requirement coverage, counterexamples, residual hazards, code-model mismatches, runtime/cost, and field transfer. The targeted gap weakens if prior studies already evaluate this complete chain across multiple systems using shared outcomes and demonstrate robust model-to-deployment transfer.
limitations: The four random papers span political opinion dynamics, robotic formal methods, value-alignment theory, and safety-analysis optimization; they do not form a homogeneous empirical field. The systematic-review follow-up was abstract-level only. This synthesis does not estimate prevalence in the full CS candidate corpus or claim the broad V&V gap is novel.
